title: Calvin: regeneration under justification possible but not necessary
source_text: XV. Quin Calvino ipsi probabile videtur locis istis ipsam regenerationem comprehendi sub justificatione, quanquam hoc non esse necesse existimet. Nam in suis in Epistolas Pauli Commentariis, exponens illud Apostoli Rom. 8. Quos vocavit, hos & justificavit; Justificatio, inquit, non male ad continuum divinae gratiae tenorem posset extendi, a Vocatione ad mortem usque: sed quia hoc verbum in tota epistola pro gratuita justitiae imputatione usurpat Paulus, nulla necessitas cogit ab hoc sensu deflectere. Et similiter ad Tit. 3. 7. haec habet: Si regenerationem accipimus proprio & usitato sensu, videri posset Apostolus justificatos ponere pro regeneratis; atque hoc aliquando significat, sed rarius. Nulla tamen necessitas cogit a propria & magis genuina significatione discedere. Et paulo post, Hoc quidem constat, Paulum justificationem asserere gratuitum esse Dei donum: tantum quaeritur quid per nomen justificationis significet. Contextus videtur postulare ut longius quam ad justitiae imputationem extendatur: in quo sensu rare, ut dixi, invenitur apud Paulum. Nihil tamen impedit quin ad remissionem peccatorum possit restringi.
pass_a_gloss: Nay, to Calvin himself it seems probable that in those places regeneration itself is comprehended under justification, although he thinks this is not necessary. For in his Commentaries on Paul's Epistles, explaining that of the Apostle Rom. 8, Whom he called, those he also justified: Justification, he says, could not badly be extended to the continuous tenor of divine grace, from Calling even unto death: but because Paul throughout the whole epistle uses this word for the gratuitous imputation of righteousness, no necessity compels us to turn aside from this sense. And likewise on Tit. 3:7 he has this: If we take regeneration in its proper and usual sense, the Apostle might seem to put the justified for the regenerate; and this it sometimes signifies, but more rarely. Yet no necessity compels us to depart from the proper and more genuine signification. And a little later: This indeed is settled, that Paul asserts justification to be a free gift of God: it is only asked what he signifies by the name of justification. The context seems to demand that it be extended further than to the imputation of righteousness: in which sense, as I have said, it is rarely found in Paul. Yet nothing prevents it from being restricted to the remission of sins.
pass_b_english: Calvin: Rom 8 / Tit 3 could stretch justification to regeneration's continuous grace—but usual Pauline sense is free imputation.
He allows rare wider use; nothing blocks restricting to remission.

choices.why: Optional wider scope vs default imputation.
